foal.e: From Middle English ffoole, foale, fole, fool, foole, fowle, from Old English fola, from Proto-West Germanic *folō, from Proto-Germanic *fulô (“foal”), from pre-Germanic *pl̥Hon-, from Proto-Indo-European *pōlH- (“animal young”).
foal.g: A young horse or similar young equine, especially just after birth or less than a year old.

foam.e: From Middle English fom, foom, from Old English fām, from Proto-West Germanic *faim, from Proto-Germanic *faimaz, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)poHy-m-os, from *(s)poH(y)- (“foam”).
foam.g: A substance composed of a large collection of bubbles or their solidified remains, especially

focus.e: Borrowed from Latin focus (“hearth, fireplace”); see there for more. Kepler introduced the term into mathematics and the sciences in describing elliptical orbits of planets (quote from Nicholas Mee): "One of the interesting properties of an ellipse is that if there were a light bulb at one focus.
focus.g: A point at which reflected or refracted rays of light converge.

fodder.e: From Middle English fodder, foder, from Old English fōdor (“feed; fodder”), from Proto-West Germanic *fōdr, from Proto-Germanic *fōdrą, from *fōdô (“food”), from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂- (“to guard, graze, feed”).
fodder.g: Food for animals; that which is fed to cattle, horses, and sheep, such as hay, cornstalks, vegetables, etc.

foe.e: From Middle English fo (“foe; hostile”), from earlier yfoh, yvo, ifa (“foe”), from Old English ġefāh (“enemy”), from fāh (“hostile”), from Proto-West Germanic *faih, from Proto-Germanic *faihaz (compare Old Frisian fāch (“punishable”), Middle High German gevēch (“feuder”)).
Acronym of fifty-one ergs, due to equalling 10⁵¹ ergs; coined by Gerald Brown of Stony Brook University in his work with Hans Bethe.
foe.g: A unit of energy equal to 10⁴⁴ joules.

foil.e: From Middle English foyle, from Middle French fueille, from Old French fueille (“plant leaf”), from Late Latin folia, the plural of folium, mistaken as a singular feminine. The literary sense is from the practice of backing a gem with metal foil to make it shine more brilliantly.
foil.g: A very thin sheet of metal.

foil.e: From Middle English foilen (“spoil a scent trail by crossing it”), from Old French fouler (“tread on, trample”), ultimately from Latin fullō (“to trample, full”).

fold.e: From Middle English folde, from Old English folde (“earth, land, country, district, region, territory, ground, soil, clay”), from Proto-Germanic *fuldǭ, *fuldō (“earth, ground; field; the world”).

foliage.e: From earlier foilage, from Late Middle English ffoylage, from Middle French feuillage. The more recent form is influenced by Latin folium (“leaf”).

folk.e: From Middle English folk, from Old English folc, from Proto-West Germanic *folk, from Proto-Germanic *fulką, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₁-gós, from *pleh₁- (“to fill”).
folk.g: A people; a tribe or nation; the inhabitants of a region, especially the native inhabitants.

folks.e: Coined by California historian Kevin Starr.
folks.g: Late 19th and early 20th century migrants to California from Iowa and other parts of the Midwestern United States.

follow.e: From Middle English folwen, folȝen, folgen, from Old English folgian (“to follow, pursue”), from Proto-West Germanic *folgēn, from Proto-Germanic *fulgāną (“to follow”).
follow.g: To go after; to pursue; to move behind in the same path or direction, especially with the intent of catching.

follower.e: From Middle English folwer, folwere, folewer, from Old English folgere (“follower; attendant; disciple”), equivalent to follow + -er.
follower.g: One who follows, comes after another.

following.g: Coming next, either in sequence or in time.

folly.e: From Middle English folie, from Old French folie (“madness”), from the adjective fol (“mad, insane”).
folly.g: Foolishness that results from a lack of foresight or lack of practicality.

folly.e: Uncertain. The most common theory is that term primarily denotes a clump of trees and relates to French feuille, feuillée and English foliage.
folly.g: A clump of trees, particularly one on the crest of a hill (or sometimes on a stretch of open ground).

fond.e: From Middle English fond, fonned, past participle of fonnen (“to be foolish, be simple, dote”), equivalent to fon + -ed.
From French, ultimately from Latin fundus.

food.e: From Middle English fode, foode, from Old English fōda (“food”), from Proto-West Germanic *fōdō, from Proto-Germanic *fōdô (“food”), from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂- (“to guard, graze, feed”).
food.g: Any solid substance that can be consumed by living organisms, especially by eating, in order to sustain life.

fool.e: From Middle English fol (“fool”), from Old French fol (cf. modern French fou (“mad”)) from Latin follis.
fool.g: A person with poor judgment or little intelligence.
A type of dessert made of puréed fruit and custard or cream.

foolish.e: From Middle English folisch; equivalent to fool + -ish.
foolish.g: Lacking good sense or judgement as a general trait; unwise; stupid.

foolishly.e: From Middle English folysly, folysschly; equivalent to foolish + -ly.

foolishness.e: From Middle English folishnesse, follissnesse, equivalent to foolish + -ness.

foot.e: From Middle English fot, fote, foot, from Old English fōt, from Proto-West Germanic *fōt, from Proto-Germanic *fōts, from Proto-Indo-European *pṓds. The plural feet is the result of i-umlaut in Proto-West Germanic *fōti, see more at Old English fōt.
foot.g: A biological structure found in many animals that is used for locomotion and that is frequently a separate organ at the terminal part of the

foothold.g: A solid grip with the feet.

footing.e: From Middle English fotyng; equivalent to foot + -ing.
footing.g: A ground for the foot; place for the foot to rest on; firm foundation to stand on.

footprint.g: The impression of the foot in a soft substance such as sand or snow.

footstep.e: From Middle English fotstep, fotstappe, from Old English *fōtstepe, *fōtstæpe (attested only in derivative fōtstappel (“footstep”)), equivalent to foot + step.
footstep.g: The mark or impression left by a foot; a track.

footstool.g: A low stool for supporting the feet while seated.

forage.e: From Middle English forage, from Old French fourage, forage, a derivative of fuerre (“fodder, straw”), from Frankish *fōdar (“fodder, sheath”), from Proto-Germanic *fōdrą (“fodder, feed, sheath”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂- (“to protect, to feed”).
forage.g: Fodder for animals, especially cattle and horses.

forasmuch.e: From Middle English for-as-moche, vor asemoche, for as miche, equivalent to for + as + much.

forbear.e: From Middle English forberen, from Old English forberan (“to forbear, abstain from, refrain; suffer, endure, tolerate, humor; restrain; do without”), from Proto-Germanic *fraberaną (“to hold back, endure”); equivalent to for- + bear.
forbear.g: To keep away from; to avoid; to abstain from.

forbearance.e: From forbear (“to keep away from, avoid”) + -ance (suffix forming nouns indicating conditions or states).
forbearance.g: The action of forbearing (“abstaining or refraining from doing something”); (countable) an instance of this.

forbearing.e: From Middle English forbering, forberyng, vorberinge, equivalent to forbear + -ing.

forbid.e: From Middle English forbeden, from Old English forbēodan (“to forbid, prohibit, restrain, refuse, repeal, annul”), from Proto-Germanic *furibeudaną, from *furi + *beudaną. Equivalent to for- (“from, away”) + bid (“to offer, proclaim”).

forbidden.e: Past participle of the verb forbid.

forbidding.g: Appearing to be threatening, unfriendly or potentially unpleasant.

force.e: From Middle English force, fors, forse, from Old French force, from Late Latin fortia, a noun derived from the neuter plural of Latin fortis (“strong”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerǵʰ- (“to rise, high, hill”).
force.g: Ability to influence; strength or energy of body or mind; active power; vigour; might; capacity of exercising an influence or producing an e

force.e: From Middle English forcen, from Old French forcier, from Late Latin *fortiāre, from Latin fortia.
force.g: To make someone or something do something, often regardless of their will.

forceful.g: Capable of either physical or coercive force; powerful.

forcible.e: From Middle English forcible, forsable, from Old French forcible, from forcier (“to conquer by force”), equivalent to force + -ible.

forcibly.e: From Middle English forceably, equivalent to forcible + -ly.
forcibly.g: In a forcible manner, by force, against one's will.

forcing.g: The act by which someone or something is forced.

ford.e: From Middle English fōrd, from Old English ford, from Proto-West Germanic *furdu, from Proto-Germanic *furduz, from Proto-Indo-European *pértus (“crossing”).
ford.g: A location where a stream is shallow and the bottom has good footing, making it possible to cross from one side to the other with no bridge,

forecast.e: From Middle English forecasten, forcasten, equivalent to fore- + cast.
forecast.g: To estimate how something will be in the future.

forefather.e: From Middle English forefader, forfader, vorvader, from Old English forefæder (“forefather”), but possibly also merged with Old Norse forfaðir. Equivalent to fore- + father.

forefinger.e: Mid-15th century, from Middle English forefynger; equivalent to fore- + finger.
forefinger.g: The index finger: the first finger next to the thumb.

forefront.e: From Middle English forefrount, forfrount, forefronte, equivalent to fore- + front.

forehead.e: From Middle English forhed, forheed, from Old English forehēafod, from Proto-West Germanic *forēhaubid, corresponding to fore- + head.
forehead.g: The part of the face above the eyebrows and below the hairline.

foreign.e: From Middle English foreyn, forein, from Old French forain, from Vulgar Latin *forānus (“outsider, outlander”), from Latin forās (“outside, outdoors”) or forīs (“outside, outdoors”). The silent -g- added perhaps by analogy with reign (compare also sovereign which was similarly altered).
foreign.g: Located outside a country or place, especially one's own.

foreigner.e: From Middle English forner, foreyner, foroner, forenere, augmentation of earlier forein (“foreigner”), from the adjective. Equivalent to foreign + -er. Use of the -er suffix may be due to analogy with Middle English straunger (“stranger”).
foreigner.g: A person from a foreign country.

foreknow.e: From Middle English forknowen (since Chaucer), a calque from praescio equivalent to fore- + know. Replaced Old English fōrwitan, fōrewitan (“to foreknow”).

foreman.e: From Middle English foremon, forman. By surface analysis, fore- + man.

foremost.e: From Old English formest, fyrmest (“earliest, first, most prominent”), from Proto-Germanic *frumistaz, from the locative stem *fur-, *fr- + the superlative suffix *-umistaz, stem ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pr-.
foremost.g: Positioned in front of (all) others in space, most forward.

foreordain.e: From Middle English for-orden; equivalent to fore- + ordain; probably modeled on Latin praeordināre.

forepart.e: From Middle English foreparte, forparte, forpart, equivalent to fore- + part.
forepart.g: The front or anterior part of something.

forerunner.e: From Middle English forrenner, foreriner. Calque of Latin praecursor (“one who runs before, a forerunner”). Equivalent to fore- + runner and/or forerun + -er.
forerunner.g: A runner at the front or ahead.

foresail.g: The lowest (and usually the largest) square sail hung on the foremast

foresee.e: From Middle English foreseen, forseen, from Old English foresēon; equivalent to fore- + see. Similar formations in Dutch voorzien, German vorsehen, Latin prōvideō, (whence provide and purvey), Ancient Greek πρόοιδα (próoida), Polish przewidzieć, Russian провидеть (providetʹ).
foresee.g: To perceive (a situation or event) in advance.

foreship.g: The fore part of a ship.

foresight.e: From Middle English forsight, forsyght, forsichte (since 14th c.), a calque of Latin providentia. By surface analysis, fore- + sight.
foresight.g: The ability, or the due use of one's ability, to foresee or prepare wisely for the future.

foreskin.e: From fore- + skin, a loose calque of Latin praepūtium.
foreskin.g: The nerve-dense, retractable fold of skin which covers and protects the glans of the penis in humans and some other mammals.

forest.e: From Middle English forest, from Old French forest, from Early Medieval Latin forestis. The Latin could be: from foris (“outside”), as in forestis (silva) "(wood) outside," or from Frankish or Proto-West Germanic *furhisti (“forest, fir-grove, wooded land”), equivalent to fir + hurst.
forest.g: A dense uncultivated tract of trees and undergrowth, larger than woods.

foretell.e: First use appears before 1400, from Middle English foretellen, equivalent to fore- + tell.
foretell.g: To predict; to tell (the future) before it occurs; to prophesy.

forever.e: Univerbation of for ever, from Middle English for ever, for evere. By surface analysis, for + ever. Noun first attested in 1858.
forever.g: For all time, for all eternity; for a lifetime; for an infinite amount of time.

forevermore.e: Compound of for + evermore, modeled after forever (for + ever).
forevermore.g: At any or all times in the future; forever.

forewarn.e: Early 14th century, from Middle English *forewarnen (suggested by Middle English forewarned, forewarning, forewarner, etc.), from Old English forewarnian (“to take warning beforehand; forewarn”), from Proto-Germanic *furawarnōną (“to forewarn”), equivalent to fore- + warn.

forfeit.e: From Middle English forfait from ca. 1300, from Old French forfait (“crime”), originally the past participle of forfaire (“to transgress”), and Medieval Latin foris factum. During the 15th century, the sense shifted from the crime to the penalty for the crime.
forfeit.g: A penalty for or consequence of a misdemeanor.

forge.e: From Middle English forge, from Old French forge, early Old French faverge, from Latin fabrica (“workshop”), from faber (“workman in hard materials, smith”) (genitive fabri). Partially displaced English smithy. Computing sense perhaps derived from the early SourceForge service, launched in 1999.
forge.g: A furnace or hearth where metals are heated prior to hammering them into shape.

forge.e: From Middle English forgen, from Anglo-Norman forger and Old French forgier, from Latin fabrico (“to frame, construct, build”).
forge.g: To shape a metal by heating and hammering.

forger.e: From Middle English forger, forgere, from Old French forgiere; equivalent to forge + -er.
forger.g: A person who creates forgeries, falsifies documents with intent to defraud, e.g. to create a false will or illicit copies of currency; count

forget.e: From Middle English forgeten, forgiten, foryeten, forȝiten, from Old English forġietan (“to forget”), from Proto-West Germanic *fragetan (“to give up, forget”). Equivalent to for- + get.

forgetful.e: From Middle English *forgetful, *forȝetful (suggested by derivative forgetfulnesse, forȝetfulnesse (“forgetfulness”)), equivalent to forget + -ful.
forgetful.g: Unable to remember things well; liable to forget.

forgetfulness.e: From Middle English forgetfulnes, forgetfulnesse, forȝetfulnesse, equivalent to forgetful + -ness.
forgetfulness.g: The quality of being forgetful; proneness to let slip from the mind.

forgive.e: Alteration (due to give) of Middle English foryiven, forȝiven, from Old English forġiefan (“to forgive, to give”), from Proto-West Germanic *frageban, from Proto-Germanic *fragebaną (“to give away; give up; release; forgive”), equivalent to for- + give (etymologically for- + yive).
forgive.g: To pardon (someone); to waive any negative feeling towards or desire for punishment or retribution against.

forgiveness.e: From Middle English forgiveness, forgifnes, from Old English forġiefnes. By surface analysis, forgive + -ness.

forgotten.e: From Middle English foryoten, from Old English forġeten, from Proto-West Germanic *fragetan. By surface analysis, forgot + -en.
forgotten.g: Of which knowledge has been lost; which is no longer remembered.

fork.e: From Middle English forke (“digging fork”), from Old English force, forca (“forked instrument used to torture”), from Proto-West Germanic *furkō (“fork”), from Latin furca (“pitchfork, forked stake; gallows, beam, stake, support post, yoke”), of uncertain origin.
fork.g: Any of several types of pronged (tined) tools (physical tools), as follows:

form.e: From Middle English forme (“shape, figure, manner, bench, frame, seat, condition, agreement, etc.”), borrowed from Old French forme, from Latin fōrma (“shape, figure, image, outline, plan, mold, frame, case, etc., manner, sort, kind, etc.”).

formation.e: From Middle English formacioun, formation, borrowed from Old French formacion, from Latin fōrmātiō, from fōrmō (“form”, verb); see form as verb. Morphologically form + -ation.
formation.g: The act of assembling a group or structure.

former.e: From Middle English former, comparative of forme (“first”), from Old English forma (“first”), descended from Proto-Germanic *frumô. Parallel to prior (via Latin), as comparative form from same Proto-Indo-European root.
From Middle English formere. By surface analysis, form + -er.
former.g: Someone who forms something; a maker; a creator or founder.

formula.e: Borrowed from Latin fōrmula (“a small pattern or mold, form, rule, principle, method, formula”), diminutive of forma (“a form”).

fornication.e: From Middle English fornicacioun, from Old French fornicacion, from Latin fornicātiō, from fornix (“brothel”).
fornication.g: Sexual intercourse by people who are not married to each other, or which is considered illicit in another way.

fornicator.e: From Middle English fornicatour, from Medieval Latin fornicātor.
fornicator.g: An unmarried person who engages in sexual intercourse, especially when considered to be of an illicit or illegal nature.

forsake.e: From Middle English forsaken (“to abandon, desert, repudiate, withdraw allegiance from”), from Old English forsacan (“to oppose; to give up, renounce; to decline, refuse”), from Proto-West Germanic *frasakan (“to forsake, renounce”). By surface analysis, for- + sake.
forsake.g: To abandon, to give up, to leave (permanently), to renounce (someone or something).

forsomuch.e: From Middle English forsomuch, equivalent to for + so + much.

forswear.e: From Middle English forsweren, from Old English forswerian (“to swear falsely”).
forswear.g: To renounce or deny something, especially under oath.

fort.e: From Middle English fort, from Middle French fort (“strong”) (adjective use is from Old French).
fort.g: A fortified defensive structure stationed with troops.

forth.e: From Middle English forth, from Old English forþ, from Proto-West Germanic *forþ, from Proto-Germanic *furþą, from Proto-Indo-European *pŕ̥-to-, from *per-.
forth.g: Forward in time, place or degree.

forthwith.e: From Middle English forth-with (“at once, immediately; at the same time, already; straight ahead”), partly from the phrase forth with (something), and partly from forth-with-al, furth-with-al (“at once, immediately; together with”) (whence forthwithal).

fortieth.e: From earlier fourteth, from Middle English fourtithe, fourtiþe; equivalent to forty + -eth. For the modern form, see the etymological notes at twentieth.
fortieth.g: The ordinal form of the number forty.

fortification.e: Borrowed from Middle French fortification, from Late Latin fortificatio, fortificationem, from fortifico, from Latin fortis. By surface analysis, fort + -ification.
fortification.g: The act of fortifying; the art or science of fortifying places to strengthen defence against an enemy.

fortify.e: From Late Middle English fortifien, fortfien (“to strengthen (a castle, etc.) from attack; to strengthen (an army, etc.); to strengthen (a person), aid, support; to reinforce, support; to improve; to increase the efficacy of”), from Old French fortifier (modern French fortifier), from Late Latin fortificāre (“to strengthen, fortify”).
fortify.g: To give power, strength, or vigour to (oneself or someone, or to something); to strengthen.

fortress.e: Early 14 c., from Old French forteresce, forteresse, forterece (“strong place, fortification”), variant of fortelesse, from Medieval Latin fortalitia, from Latin fortis (“strong”) (see fort) + -itia, added to adjectives to form nouns of quality or condition. French -ess, from Latin -itia is also in words such as duress, prowess, largesse and richesse.
fortress.g: A fortified place; a large and permanent fortification, sometimes including a town; for example a fort, a castle; a stronghold; a place of d

fortunate.e: From Middle English fortunat(e) (“fortunate”), from Latin fortūnātus, from fortūna (“fortune, luck”) + -ātus (adjective-forming suffix), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix). By surface analysis, fortune + -ate.

fortune.e: From Middle English fortune, from Old French fortune, from Latin fortuna (“fate, luck”). The plural form fortunae meant “possessions”, which also gave fortune the meaning of “riches”.

forty.e: From Middle English fourty, forty, from Old English fēowertiġ, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *fedwōr tigiwiz (“forty”). By surface analysis, four + -ty.
forty.g: The cardinal number occurring after thirty-nine and before forty-one, represented in Roman numerals as XL and in Arabic numerals as 40.
Resembling or characteristic of a fort.

forum.e: From Latin forum (“public market place, forum”).

forward.e: From Middle English foreward, from Old English foreweard (“forward, inclined to the front, fore, early, former”), from Proto-Germanic *fura- (“fore-”), *warþaz (“turned”), equivalent to fore + -ward.
forward.g: Situated toward or at the front of something.

forward.e: From Middle English foreward, from Old English foreweard (“condition, bargain, agreement, contract, treaty, assurance”), equivalent to fore- + ward (“ward, keeping”).

foster.e: From Middle English foster, from Old English fōstor (“food, sustenance”), from Proto-West Germanic *fōstr, from Proto-Germanic *fōstrą (“nourishment, food”).
foster.g: Providing parental care to children not related to oneself.

foul.e: From Middle English ffoul, foul, foull, fowel, fowle, fuyle, voul, vul, from Old English fūl (“foul, dirty, unclean, impure, vile, corrupt, rotten, stinking, guilty”), from Proto-West Germanic *fūl, from Proto-Germanic *fūlaz (“foul, rotten”), from Proto-Indo-European *puH- (“foul, rotten”).
foul.g: Covered with, or containing unclean matter; dirty.

foul.e: From Middle English foulen, fulen, from Old English fūlian (“to become foul; rot; decay”), from Proto-West Germanic *fūlēn, from Proto-Germanic *fūlāną (“to rot; decay”).

found.e: From Middle English founden, from Old French founder (Modern French: fonder), from Latin fundāre.
From Middle English founden, from Old French fondre, from Latin fundere.
found.g: To melt, especially of metal or glass in an industrial setting.

foundation.e: From Middle English foundacioun, fundacioun, from Old French fondacion, from Latin fundātiō (“founding, foundation”).
foundation.g: The act of founding, fixing, establishing, or beginning to erect.

founder.e: From Middle English foundour, from Old French fondeur, from Latin fundātor, equivalent to found + -er.
founder.g: One who founds or establishes (a company, project, organisation, state, etc.).

founder.e: From Middle French fondrer (“send to the bottom”), from Latin fundus (“bottom”).
founder.g: A severe laminitis of a horse, caused by untreated internal inflammation in the hooves.

fount.e: Clipping of fountain, on the pattern of the pair mount, mountain.
fount.g: Synonym of fountain (“a natural source of water”); a spring.

fount.e: A variant of font, influenced by fount (etymology 1) being a synonym of font (“natural source of water, spring”).

fountain.e: From Middle English; from Old French fontaine (whence modern fontaine); from Late Latin fontana, from Latin fontanus, fontaneus, adjectives from fons (“source, spring”).
fountain.g: A natural source of water; a spring.

four.e: From Middle English four, from Old English fēower, from Proto-West Germanic *feuwar, from Proto-Germanic *fedwōr, from previous pre-Grimm *petwṓr, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwṓr, the neuter form of *kʷetwóres.
four.g: A numerical value equal to 4; the number following three and preceding five.

fourfold.e: From Middle English fourfold, fourefold, from Old English fēowerfeald. Equivalent to four + -fold.

foursquare.e: From Middle English foure square; equivalent to four + square.

fourteen.e: From Middle English fourtene, from Old English fēowertīene, from Proto-Germanic *fedurtehun. Equivalent to four + -teen.
fourteen.g: The cardinal number occurring after thirteen and before fifteen.

fourteenth.e: From Middle English fourtenthe, fourtethe, from Old English fēowertēoþa, equivalent to fourteen + -th.
fourteenth.g: The ordinal form of the number fourteen.

fourth.e: From Middle English fourthe, an alteration (due to four) of ferthe, from Old English fēorþa, fēowerþa, from Proto-West Germanic *feurþō, from Proto-Germanic *fedurþô, equivalent to four + -th (ordinal suffix).
fourth.g: The ordinal form of the number four.

fowl.e: From Middle English foul, foghel, fowel, fowele, from Old English fugol (“bird”), from Proto-West Germanic *fugl, from Proto-Germanic *fuglaz, dissimilated variant of *fluglaz (compare Old English flugol ‘fleeing’, Mercian fluglas heofun ‘birds of the air’), from *fleuganą (“to fly”).

fowler.e: From Middle English foulere, fouler, from Old English fuglere (“fowler”), from Proto-West Germanic *fuglārī, equivalent to fowl + -er.

fox.e: From Middle English fox, from Old English fox (“fox”), from Proto-West Germanic *fuhs, from Proto-Germanic *fuhsaz (“fox”), from Proto-Indo-European *púḱsos (“the tailed one”), possibly from *puḱ- (“tail”). Philosophical sense from the 1953 essay The Hedgehog and the Fox by Isaiah Berlin.
fox.g: A small-to-medium-sized canine mammal, related to dogs and wolves, with a flattened skull, upright triangular ears, a pointed, slightly uptu

fight.e: From Middle English fighten (“to fight”), from Old English feohtan (“to fight, combat, strive”), from Proto-West Germanic *fehtan (“to fight”), from Proto-Germanic *fehtaną (“to comb, tease, shear, struggle with”), from Proto-Indo-European *peḱ- (“to comb, shear”). Related also to Old English feht (“wool, shaggy pelt, fleece”).

From Middle English fight, feyght, fiȝt, fecht, from Old English feoht, ġefeoht (“fight”), from Proto-West Germanic *fehtan (“to fight”), from Proto-Germanic *fehtą, *gafehtą (“fight, struggle”), from Proto-Germanic *fehtaną (“to struggle with”).
